newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Glaverbel sees better 97 operating result.
newsitem.headline: Glaverbel sees better 97 operating result.

text.p: Belgian glass maker Glaverbel said on Thursday it expected to see improved operating results and a further decrease of financial charges in 1997.
"Given the continuing upturn in European glass consumption and assuming prices hold up the group anticipates an improvement in its operating result in 1997, Glaverbel said in a statement.

Chief executive officer Luc Willame told a news conference, at which the company presented 1996 results, that Glaverbel was "reasonably confident" for 1997. "Unless there's something new on the currency front or a big price drop, there should be an improvement in profit," he added.

In 1996 Glaverbel's operating profit fell to 2.732 billion francs from 2.987 billion in 1995 after severe recession in the first half of last year when raw glass volumes and prices fell. Volumes picked up in the second half of 1996, but not prices.

Willame said the price drop had wiped one billion francs off 1996 turnover, which edged up one percent at 38.663 billion francs, though 70 to 80 percent of this negative effect was clawed back via increased volume and productivity.
Glaverbel made a 1996 group net profit of 1.768 billion francs, up from 621 million in 1995 and boosted by extraordinary profit of 606 million francs.
Operating results in 1997 would be helped by growth in European glass consumption estimated at two percent overall, and expected to be strongest in the automotive sector.

Glaverbel said its past investment programme was starting to pay off. "We now have the most modern production equipment in Europe," Willame said. Future investments would concentrate on providing "added value".

The company predicted 100 percent activity for 1997 at its Glavunion unit, after a six-month long repair of its float line in 1996. This year would see the repair of the float line at its Maasglas subsidiary in the Netherlands.
Glaverbel expected to decrease financial charges further in 1997 through debt control and the impact of interest rates which it expected to remain low.
Generally, Glaverbel said its strategy was to "grow in a profitable way" according to its financial resources, and to pursue its geographical diversification.
One of the company's biggest challenges was tackling low profitability in its processing activities, especially in Belgium which suffered high labour costs.
